summary: OpenAI's Toki Sherbakov and Prashant Mital describe how the Technical Success team helps enterprises deploy AI. OpenAI has two core engineering teams: 1,200 researchers building foundational models, and a product team creating ChatGPT and the API. The go-to-market team deploys these into customer environments and feeds field insights back to research. The enterprise AI customer journey has three phases: building an AI-enabled workforce (ChatGPT), automating internal operations (API for custom use cases), and infusing AI into end-user products (primarily API). Strategy should start top-down, aligning AI to broader business strategy rather than treating AI as a standalone initiative, then identifying one to two high-impact use cases and building divisional capability through enablement, centers of excellence, and centralized platforms. A typical use case spans roughly three months: ideation, scoping, architecture review, defining KPIs, iterative development, testing and evaluation with A/B testing, production launch, and maintenance. OpenAI partners via workshops, office hours, paired programming, early model access, internal experts, and joint roadmap sessions. The Morgan Stanley case study involved an internal knowledge assistant for wealth managers; starting at 45% accuracy, iterative methods including hybrid retrieval, fine-tuning, chunking, reranking, classification, prompt engineering, and query expansion pushed accuracy to 98%, exceeding the 90% goal. Prashant defines an agent as a model with instructions, tools, and an execution loop with model-controlled termination. Four field lessons follow. First, abstraction is a tool, not a crutch: build with primitives first and introduce abstraction only when reinventing the wheel. Second, start simple: deploy a single purpose-built agent for one task with a limited user set, observe real bottlenecks like hallucinations, latency, or poor retrieval, then incrementally improve. Third, use a network of agents with handoffs for complex tasks: specialized agents handle subflows, and handoffs transfer control while preserving full conversation history. A customer service example uses GPT-4o mini for triage, GPT-4o for conversation management, and o3 mini for accuracy-sensitive refund eligibility checks. Fourth, keep prompts simple and focused on the target task; run guardrails in parallel using faster, cheaper models, and defer high-stakes tool calls until all guardrails return. Guardrails enforce safety, security, and reliability without complicating the main prompt.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and OpenAI structure
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves and OpenAI's operating model: 1,200 researchers build foundational models, a product team turns these into ChatGPT and the API, and the go-to-market team deploys products to customers and feeds field insights back to research.

sections.title: Enterprise AI customer journey
sections.summary: Describes three phases: building an AI-enabled workforce (ChatGPT), automating internal operations (API for custom use cases), and infusing AI into end-user products (primarily API). Phases need not happen strictly in sequence.

sections.title: AI as part of business strategy
sections.summary: Strategy should be top-down, aligning AI to the broader business strategy. Identify one to two high-impact use cases, scope them, then build divisional capability through enablement and centers of excellence. Typical use case journey spans ideation, scoping, architecture review, KPI definition, iterative development, testing, production, and maintenance. OpenAI partners via workshops, office hours, paired programming, early model access, and joint roadmap sessions.

sections.title: Morgan Stanley case study
sections.summary: Morgan Stanley built an internal knowledge assistant for wealth managers querying research reports and stock data. Starting accuracy was 45%. Iterative methods including hybrid retrieval, fine-tuning, chunking, reranking, classification, prompt engineering, and query expansion pushed accuracy to 98%, exceeding their 90% goal.

sections.title: 2025 year of agents and agent definition
sections.summary: Declares 2025 the year of agents where AI graduates from assistant to collaborator. Defines an agent as a model with instructions, tools for retrieving information and interacting with external systems, encapsulated in an execution loop whose termination is model-controlled.

sections.title: Lesson 1: Abstraction is a tool, not a crutch
sections.summary: When designing agents, starting with frameworks is enticing for fast prototypes but obscures system behavior and constraints. Better to build with primitives first, understand task decomposition and failure points, then introduce abstraction when reinventing the wheel. Choosing the right framework matters less than understanding data and failure points.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Start simple
sections.summary: Teams often jump straight into multi-agent systems, creating unknowns without insight. Instead, start with a single purpose-built agent for one task, deploy to a limited user set, observe real bottlenecks like hallucinations, latency, or poor retrieval, then incrementally improve. Complexity should increase only as failure cases and constraints demand it.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Use a network of agents for complex tasks
sections.summary: For complex tasks, use a network of specialized agents handling subflows within a larger workflow. Handoffs transfer control between agents while preserving full conversation history. A sample customer service architecture uses GPT-4o mini for triage, GPT-4o for dispute conversation management, and o3 mini for accuracy-sensitive refund eligibility checks.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Keep prompts simple; use guardrails for edge cases
sections.summary: Guardrails enforce safety, security, and reliability. Keep model instructions simple and focused on the target task for maximum interoperability and predictable accuracy improvement. Run guardrails in parallel using faster, cheaper models like GPT-4o mini rather than embedding them in main prompts. Defer high-stakes tool calls until all guardrails return.

sections.title: Recap
sections.summary: Recaps four lessons: use abstractions minimally, start with a single agent, graduate to a network of agents when needed, and keep prompts simple while using guardrails to handle edge cases.
